h1: No and low alcohol beer for commercial teams
title: No and Low Alcohol Beer Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What no and low alcohol beer is, how it is made and why it behaves differently in pricing, shelf life and sales data.
teaser: A 0.5% beer looks like a normal beer in the dashboard. On the floor and on the shelf it is a different product.
standfirst: No and low alcohol beer sits inside beer portfolios but plays by its own rules. Here is what commercial teams need to know about how it is made, labelled and sold before they build a plan around it.
sections: Low alcohol and alcohol free mean different numbers in different places

Start with the labels, because they change the rest of the plan. In many markets "alcohol free" beer means 0.5% ABV (alcohol by volume) or less. The UK is stricter: alcohol free means no more than 0.05%, de-alcoholised means no more than 0.5% and low alcohol means no more than 1.2%. A standard Indian lager sits around 4.5 to 5%, with strong beers at 6 to 8%.

India adds a twist. Whether a product is regulated as a food or as an excisable liquor depends on its strength and on how the state treats it. A beer under the alcohol threshold usually sits under food safety law. Above it, excise takes over. The thresholds and the paperwork vary by state and change, so the regulatory team should check the current notification before anyone commits to a launch date.
There are two ways to make it and they cost differently

Brewers make no and low alcohol beer in one of two broad ways. The first is to brew a normal beer, then take the alcohol out. Vacuum distillation boils off alcohol at around 40 to 50 °C instead of 78 °C, which protects flavour. Membrane systems such as reverse osmosis filter it out cold. Both need expensive kit and add a process step.

The second way is to stop alcohol forming in the first place. The brewer makes a thin wort with fewer fermentable sugars, uses a yeast that cannot ferment maltose or cuts fermentation short by chilling. This needs no new equipment but is harder to get tasting like beer.

For a commercial team, the method matters because it sets the cost per litre and the capacity. A plant with one dealcoholisation unit has a hard ceiling on output however strong the demand. Our guide to production planning basics shows how one constrained step limits a whole line.
Shelf life is shorter and the cold chain matters more

Alcohol is a mild preservative. Take it out and the beer becomes friendlier to spoilage microbes. Most alcohol free beers are pasteurised for that reason, A standard lager is often given somewhere around 15 to 25 pasteurisation units (PU), a measure of heat over time. Alcohol free beer usually gets more. That protects the beer but can dull fresh flavour.

In a hot country this shows up in the data. A low alcohol product that sits in a 40 °C warehouse in May will lose its fresh character faster than a 5% lager next to it. If returns or complaints spike in summer for one SKU, check storage before blaming the recipe.
Pricing does not follow the excise logic of regular beer

Regular beer prices in India are heavily shaped by state excise. Our guide to how beer MRP is set state by state walks through it. A product outside the excise net can have a very different price build: less duty, but often a higher cost of goods because of the extra process step and lower volumes.

So an analyst comparing margin per case across the portfolio needs to split no and low alcohol out. Lumping it with lager will make one look worse and the other look better than either really is.
Marketing it needs care in India

Alcohol advertising is restricted in India. Brand extensions that carry a beer brand name onto a soda, water or alcohol free product are watched closely, because regulators and courts have long been wary of surrogate advertising. A genuine alcohol free product with its own distribution is a different case from a token SKU that exists mainly to put a logo on television.

None of this is legal advice. It is the reason a commercial plan for alcohol free beer should go past the legal team early. Claims matter too. Make no health claims and say nothing that suggests the product is suitable for people who should not drink at all without checking the label rules.
Taste is the hardest part to get right

Alcohol does more than carry the buzz. It adds body, a little warmth and a slight sweetness. It also helps carry hop aroma. Take it out and many beers taste thin and sweet, with a worty, cereal note that drinkers describe as unfinished. Brewers fight this with more specialty malt, careful hopping, higher carbonation and sometimes added flavour.

For a commercial team this explains two things. First, why early alcohol free products often had poor repeat purchase: people tried them once. Second, why a new recipe can change the sales curve sharply. When a brand reformulates, treat the before and after periods as different products in the data. A guided tasting of a regular lager beside its alcohol free version, with spit cups and fully optional, teaches a sales team more about this in ten minutes than any slide.
What changes in the sales data

A few patterns are worth knowing before you build a forecast:

  • Different occasions. Alcohol free beer sells at lunch, at work events and to drivers. Its weekly shape can differ from regular beer.
  • Different channels. It can often be sold where alcohol cannot, which changes the outlet list and the channel mix.
  • Smaller base. Growth percentages look large on a small base. Read volumes alongside the percentages.
  • Dry days. Depending on state rules, alcohol free products may keep selling on days when liquor sales stop. Check rather than assume.

A good first step: pull last year's sales for one alcohol free SKU and one regular lager in the same state, then plot them week by week on the same chart. Where the lines part is where your assumptions need to change.
faqs: Is alcohol free beer completely free of alcohol?
Not always. In many markets alcohol free means up to 0.5% ABV, while the UK allows only 0.05%. Always check the label and the local definition.
Why does alcohol free beer cost more to make?
Removing alcohol needs extra equipment such as vacuum distillation or membranes, plus energy and time. Volumes are also smaller, so fixed costs spread over fewer litres.
Is no and low alcohol beer taxed like regular beer in India?
It depends on its strength and on state rules. Products under the alcohol threshold usually fall under food law rather than excise, but rules vary and change, so check the current notification.
Does alcohol free beer go off faster?
It is more vulnerable to spoilage because alcohol is a mild preservative, so most are pasteurised. Heat in storage also shortens its fresh flavour life.
